extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in public policy, regulatory reform, and general nonfiction book buyers
extracted.subtask_description: A short Publishers Weekly review of Cass R. Sunstein’s book arguing principles for designing modern regulatory policy: simplicity, transparency, cost‑benefit reasoning, and behavioral nudges. The page summarizes the book’s prescriptions and gives examples of regulations implemented or repealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep regulations simple and clear
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein articulates an astonishingly straightforward regulatory philosophy that prioritizes simplicity and clarity; he contrasts this with byzantine and partisan rulemaking. Examples suggest eliminating convoluted or overly technical rules that create unnecessary compliance burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable citizen choice with information and encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: Let citizens choose while giving them information and encouragement to choose well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state should provide information and 'nudges' (drawing on behavioral economics) so individuals can make better decisions without heavy-handed mandates. Examples include mandated disclosures (airline and credit card fees) that allow consumers to choose among options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing disproportionate burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure regulations don’t impose disproportionate burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory design should seek proportionality—burdens on regulated parties should not be excessive relative to benefits. This principle underlies Sunstein’s defense of cost‑benefit thinking as a check on overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cost–benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Champion cost‑benefit analysis as a central tool for regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein 'champions the much‑maligned cost‑benefit analysis' to assess regulatory tradeoffs and prioritize interventions that provide net social gain. The review treats CBA as a core methodological recommendation for smarter regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and measure performance of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep track of how well regulations are working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations should be subject to follow‑up evaluation and empirical monitoring to determine effectiveness and justify continuation, modification, or repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply behavioral economics (nudges) to improve outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: See a role for the state in nudging humans towards rationality and responsibility using behavioral economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should use insights from behavioral economics to design encouragements and choice architectures that increase welfare without heavy coercion. Sunstein’s account grounds his prescriptions in lucid treatments of behavioral economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize cheaper, smarter, better government over size
rubrics_metrics.description: Not bigger or smaller government, but cheaper, smarter, better government is the guiding aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The normative target is improved governmental performance (efficiency and humanity), not necessarily expanding or shrinking government; policies should be evaluated on whether they make government more effective and less wasteful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish ill‑considered or absurd rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove regulations that are ill‑considered or absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein recounts examples where OIRA abolished inappropriate rules (e.g., treating industrial milk spills as if they were toxic oil spills), implying regular review and pruning of outdated or nonsensical regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate disclosure and transparency where it aids choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mandated disclosure to empower consumers (e.g., airline and credit card fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency requirements are presented as a low‑cost intervention that improves market functioning by informing consumers and enabling informed choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt targeted environmental and efficiency standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue regulations that reduce pollution and improve efficiency (examples: cutting power‑plant pollution, improving auto fuel mileage standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein’s tenure at OIRA is cited for concrete regulatory accomplishments—demonstrating that targeted standards can achieve social goals while fitting within the broader framework of simplicity, CBA, and monitoring.
